cards.text: Friend, Isaiah the prophet has been carrying a heavy message from the LORD about Babylon. Storm clouds everywhere. Then, right in the middle of it, the message turns to Jacob, the people of Israel.

cards.question: In the middle of all that, Isaiah says the LORD will have ___ on Jacob.
The LORD says He will choose Israel once again and settle them in their own land.
In this homecoming, the foreigner is kept away from the house of Jacob.

cards.text: And the nations themselves escort Israel and bring it back to its homeland. I waited YEARS for anybody to give me a ride out of a junk drawer, and these folks get an ESCORT.

cards.question: Once Israel is back in the LORD's land, what does Isaiah say they will do to their captors?

cards.text: Then Isaiah talks right to the people. On the day the LORD gives them rest from their pain and torment, and from the hard labor they were forced into, they'll sing a song of contempt.

cards.question: Isaiah says the people will sing this song of contempt against the king of ___.

cards.text: The song opens with one big exhale: "How the oppressor has ceased, and how his fury has ended!" That's the sigh I let out when a stuck oven timer FINALLY quits beeping, and I only had to put up with that for ten minutes.

cards.question: The song says the staff of the wicked, the scepter of the rulers, has been broken. Who broke it?
Before it was broken, that staff struck the peoples in anger with ___ blows.
With the oppressor's staff broken, the whole earth goes quiet and holds its breath.

cards.text: Even the cypresses and cedars of Lebanon get a line in this song, and they're talking straight to the fallen king. Friend, when the TREES are celebrating that you're gone, it's time to look in the mirror.

cards.question: Why are the cypresses and cedars of Lebanon so glad the king of Babylon has been laid low?

answers.text: The rain has finally come back
Their roots have room to grow

cards.text: Then the song goes down to Sheol, and Sheol is eager to meet him when he arrives. Friend, there are welcome parties you do NOT want thrown for you.

cards.question: Who does Sheol stir up to greet the king of Babylon?
When the king of Babylon arrives in Sheol, the kings of the nations stay seated on their thrones.
What do the dead kings in Sheol say to the king of Babylon?

answers.text: You have become weak like us
You will rule over us here
You are stronger than us all

cards.text: His pomp and the music of his harps come down to Sheol with him, where "Maggots are your bed and worms your blanket." I slept under dusty warranty cards for years, and even I'd pass on that bedding.
Then the song cries out, "How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn!" Friend, I've face-planted into a whole bowl of chocolate chips, and this fall STILL wins.

cards.question: The song says the day star has been cut down to the ground, and it calls him the ___ of nations.

cards.text: Then the song reveals what he said in his heart. And oh, friend, this man had PLANS.

cards.question: In his heart, he said he would ascend to the heavens and raise his ___ above the stars of God.

cards.text: He'd sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north, and ascend above the tops of the clouds. This man's vision board needed a CEILING.

cards.question: In his heart, what was the very top of the king's plan?

answers.text: To make himself like the Most High
To bring every captive back home
To build a temple for the LORD

cards.text: Up, up, up was the plan. But the song says this elevator is headed the other way.

cards.question: Instead of rising above the clouds, where will the king be brought down to?

answers.text: The lowest depths of the Pit

cards.text: Those who see him will stare and ponder his fate. A full, slow, wide-eyed double take.

cards.question: What do the people staring at the fallen king of Babylon ask?

answers.text: Is this the man who shook the earth
Is this the man who freed the captives
Is this the man who built our cities

cards.question: The people remember the king of Babylon as the one who let the captives return to their homes.

cards.text: Now, all the kings of the nations lie in state, each in his own tomb. Reserved spots, every one of them.

cards.question: While the other kings rest in their own tombs, what happens to the king of Babylon?

answers.text: He is cast out of his grave
He is buried with great honor
He is laid among his fathers

cards.question: Why won't the king of Babylon join the other kings in burial?

answers.text: He destroyed his land and slaughtered his people
He never built a tomb for himself
His own sons refused to bury him

cards.text: The song says the offspring of the wicked will never again be mentioned. Then comes a hard line: prepare a place to slaughter his sons for the iniquities of their forefathers.

cards.question: The king's sons will rise up, possess a land and cover the earth with their cities.

cards.text: Now the LORD speaks for Himself. "I will rise up against them," declares the LORD of Hosts.

cards.question: The LORD says He will leave Babylon a remnant to carry on her name.
The LORD says He will sweep Babylon away with the ___ of destruction.

cards.text: And the LORD says He'll make Babylon a place for owls and for swamplands. The man who planned a throne above the stars of God, and his city ends up as the OWLS' timeshare.

findings.problem: The opening card states a fact from outside the passage: Isaiah has been carrying a message from the LORD about Babylon (Isaiah 13). The card cites only Isaiah 14:1 and gives no reference for that fact.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The question opens with "In the middle of all that," which points back to card 1. Card 1 is no longer on screen when the baker answers.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The statement says "The LORD says He will choose Israel once again." In Isaiah 14:1 the LORD is not speaking. The prophet is telling what the LORD will do ("For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob; once again He will choose Israel").

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: "In this homecoming" points back to earlier cards for its context instead of saying whose homecoming it is.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: "that staff" points back to the question on card 10, which is no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The question says the staff struck "in anger." That wording rules out the wrong answers "gentle" and "occasional" on sight. "gentle" also reads as silly next to "in anger," so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The statement "the whole earth goes quiet and holds its breath" is meant to be false. But Isaiah 14:7 says the earth "is at peace and at rest," so a baker could argue that "goes quiet" is true. Only "holds its breath" conflicts with the text, which leaves the statement half true.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The joke "when the TREES are celebrating that you're gone, it's time to look in the mirror" laughs at the king of Babylon, a person in the passage, instead of at Papa Dorin or at the king's human situation.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself. Humor about people in Bible stories laughs with their human situation, never at them.

findings.problem: The question begins "In his heart, he said" and never says who "he" is. It relies on earlier cards that are no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: The joke "This man's vision board needed a CEILING" mocks the king, a person in the passage, instead of Papa Dorin.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself. Humor about people in Bible stories laughs with their human situation, never at them.

findings.problem: The punchline "The man who planned a throne above the stars of God, and his city ends up as the OWLS' timeshare" laughs at the king, a person in the passage.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself. Humor about people in Bible stories laughs with their human situation, never at them.
